title: Missing the Butterfly and Predicting the Past: Features or Bugs of Accurate AI Weather Models?
hook: AI weather models can be trained to predict the past as skillfully as the future. The same flaw that lets them do it explains why their forecasts beat physics.
key_points: AI weather models can be trained to backcast (predict the past) skillfully, though less accurately than they forecast.
Skillful backcasting appears to violate the second law of thermodynamics — there should be an arrow of time.
All the forecasting and backcasting models tested miss the butterfly effect: errors don't grow the way chaos says they should.
One cause explains both plus the surprising accuracy — coarse-graining of training data removes fast, small scales and some variables.
Reduce the coarse-graining and predictions become more physics-like (arrow of time and butterfly-like effects appear) while accuracy declines.
Tested across a hierarchy: reanalysis data, a general circulation model, and the multi-scale Lorenz system, up to Pangu-Weather.
content_html: AI weather prediction models now rival physics-based ones, and nobody was quite sure why they were so good. Hassanzadeh and colleagues find the answer by asking the models to do something they shouldn't be able to: predict the past.
extra_html:
The diagnostic

Across a hierarchy spanning observation-based reanalysis, a general circulation model, and the multi-scale Lorenz system, the authors show AI models can be trained to backcast skillfully — systematically less accurately than they forecast, but skillfully all the same. That's a problem, because skillful backcasting appears to violate the second law of thermodynamics: real atmospheric dynamics have an arrow of time. Separately, all these models — forecasting and backcasting alike — miss the butterfly effect, failing to reproduce the rapid error growth that chaos demands.

One cause, three symptoms

The paper traces the surprising accuracy, the missing butterfly, and the skillful backcasting to a single source: the inevitable coarse-graining of training data, which strips out fast, small scales and sometimes entire variables. From the Lorenz system up to official Pangu-Weather models, reducing that coarse-graining makes predictions more physics-like — an arrow of time and butterfly-like effects emerge — while forecast accuracy declines. So the forecast skill has an explanation that is also a caveat: unlike physics-based models, AI models implicitly learn how fast, small scales affect large ones without inheriting their rapid error growth. The authors argue this calls for revisiting predictability theory and long-term climate emulation strategies, and propose backcasting as a new diagnostic lens. arXiv, 2026.

related.title: GraphCast: Skillful Medium-Range Weather Forecasting
related.hook: A graph neural network predicts 10-day global weather in under a minute on one machine, matching or beating physics-based forecast models on most variables.

related.title: WeatherNext Cyclones: An Extra Day of Hurricane Warning
related.hook: DeepMind's cyclone model makes three-day forecasts as accurate as yesterday's two-day forecasts — about a decade of meteorological progress, delivered in under a minute on a TPU.

flashcards.prompt: What single cause do the authors trace the missing butterfly effect, skillful backcasting, and surprising forecast accuracy to?
flashcards.back_html: Coarse-graining of the training data, which removes fast, small scales and sometimes whole variables. The model learns how small scales affect large ones without inheriting their rapid error growth.

flashcards.prompt: What happens when the coarse-graining of the training data is reduced?

choices.text: Predictions become more physics-like — an arrow of time and butterfly-like effects emerge — but forecast accuracy declines
Both physical fidelity and forecast accuracy improve together
The models stop being able to backcast but forecast accuracy is unchanged

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper reports a direct trade-off from the Lorenz system up to official Pangu-Weather models: more physical fidelity, less forecast skill.

flashcards.prompt: Why is skillful backcasting by an AI weather model a red flag?
flashcards.back_html: It appears to violate the second law of thermodynamics. Real atmospheric dynamics have an arrow of time, so a model that runs backwards nearly as well as forwards isn't capturing that dynamics.
